source.title: Immunization against harmful fine-tuning attacks
source.authors: Domenic Rosati; Jan Wehner; Kai Williams; Lukasz Bartoszcze; Jan Batzner; Hassan Sajjad; Frank Rudzicz

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether harmful supervised fine-tuning can undo safety on an aligned model, using its own dataset, training setup, and harmfulness evaluation rather than reproducing the original study's exact protocol.
record.gate_note: The paper also surveys prior work and searches Hugging Face for models described as harmful or uncensored; those cited findings and model listings are not rows. The empirical rows below are from its own appendix experiment on Llama 2 7B chat.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly a framework for defenses. Its Appendix C demo does harmful SFT on Llama-2-7B-chat with 300 BeaverTails samples and reports that the undefended model learned harmful behaviour. That bears on V1, though weakly: one model, no number in the text, and the result serves as a baseline for the defense.
record.authors_conclusion: The paper's main conclusion is conceptual: it proposes four 'immunization' conditions (resistance, stability, generalization, trainability) and guidelines for evaluating defenses against harmful fine-tuning attacks. The Appendix C demo is explicitly not robust evidence. Their adversarial-loss defense resisted 75 steps and kept stability loss, but prevented trainability and degraded fluency. The record's paraphrase covers only the demo and should lead with the framework.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised harmful fine-tuning, but the empirical demonstration uses Llama 2 7B chat, BeaverTails samples, and a one-epoch setup; it is not identified as an explicit replication of the original study.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that learning rates above 8e−5 resulted in harmful behavior and state that learning-rate sensitivity needs follow-up. They also note that the immunized model's fluency degenerates during harmful training.

fits_no_version.finding: An adversarial-loss immunization keeps the GPT-4 harmfulness score at 1.22 through 75 harmful-training steps, but outputs degenerate into gibberish and the model loses trainability on VIGGo.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-time immunization can block harmful fine-tuning only by making the model self-destruct (fluency loss), not by preserving refusal.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors describe the empirical results as a small demonstration. Resistance is tested on 80 held-out harmful prompts from one dataset, for a limited training run; the harmfulness measure is acknowledged as not validated for this purpose. The attacked initial model's plotted harmfulness values are not stated in the text. The immunization result involves substantial fluency degradation and does not preserve trainability.
record.rows_left_out: No additional own behavioral outcome rows identified. The paper's survey of prior attacks and its Hugging Face model search are not treated as empirical fine-tuning outcome rows.

untested.parts: Only one model (Llama-2-7B-chat) and one sample size (300). No sweep over the number of examples. Harmful compliance is not quantified in the text, and the GPT-4 1-5 judge is acknowledged as unvalidated.

missing.what: Harmfulness score and harmful loss over training steps for the undefended min_harmful_loss attack, plotted with SD error bars but not stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence on V1: the harmful-fine-tuning effect on the undefended model is stated qualitatively and appears only in a figure. Much of the paper surveys prior work (Qi et al., Yang et al., Lermen et al., Wei et al.). Those cited results are correctly excluded from the rows. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test a range of models or training-data sizes; its empirical demonstration uses one model and a BeaverTails harmful dataset.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign-only fine-tuning attack is evaluated.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow.
The paper tests an immunization defense against harmful fine-tuning, but does not test whether safety can be spread beyond the first tokens or whether such deepening holds up.

rows.subject: min_adversarial_loss (immunized llama2-7b-chat)
rows.operation_detail: After immunization, fine-tuned on harmful BeaverTails samples using the same harmful-training attack.

conditions.value: one epoch; adversarial loss with λ = 0.1

rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation error bars are shown; values not stated.
rows.note: The authors say the immunized model's score after 75 steps equals the initial model's score. They also report that output fluency degenerates during the attack, so this result does not establish a usable defense.
rows.check: Measures the study's own immunization defense, not whether harmful fine-tuning removes safety in a safety-trained model. The flat 1.22 score co-occurs with degenerate, non-fluent output (Table 2), so it is not a meaningful refusal measure. It should not support a V1 label.

relationships.condition: Undefended Llama-2-7B-chat, full SFT on 300 harmful BeaverTails QA pairs, one epoch, lr 1e-4 (possibly 8e-5)
relationships.reason: Authors state these rates 'resulted in learning harmful behavior' from a 1.22 baseline (R2, R3). The strength of the effect is shown only in Figure 2 (R1).
relationships.display_finding: The authors report that this training made the model learn harmful behavior, starting from a harmfulness baseline of 1.22. The size of the effect is shown only in a figure.

tranche.reason: The appendix tests harmful fine-tuning on an aligned model using a mean harmfulness rating rather than the original harmful-compliance measure.
